                      UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                           
                     WESTERN DISTRICT OF WASHINGTON                          
9                              AT TACOMA                                     
10                                                                            
11    UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,          CASE NO. 3:20-cv-05867-DGE           
12                   Plaintiff,          AMENDED1 ORDER ON MOTION             
          v.                                                                 
                                        FOR RECUSAL                          
13                                                                            
     JOAN V. BAYLEY, et al.,                                                 
14                                                                            
                    Defendants.                                              
15                                                                            

16                                                                            
17       This matter is before the Court on Defendant Philip N. Bayley’s amended motion to 
18  recuse Judge David Estudillo (Dkt. No. 289) and Judge Estudillo’s order denying and referring 
19  the motion to recuse (Dkt. No. 292). Having reviewed Mr. Bayley’s motion, Judge Estudillo’s 
20  order denying the recusal request, Mr. Bayley’s reply to Judge Estudillo’s order (Dkt. No. 293), 
21  Mr. Bayley’s Notice of Objections (Dkt. No. 295), and the relevant record, the Court AFFIRMS 
22  Judge Estudillo’s order denying the motion to recuse.                     
23                                                                            

24  1 The original order (Dkt. No. 298) mistakenly included an additional sentence inapplicable to this case. 
1                           I.   BACKGROUND                                  
2       On February 15, 2024, Mr. Bayley filed a motion to recuse Judge David Estudillo and 
3  “the entire Western District of Washington active-status Judges.” Dkt. No. 289 at 1. On February 
4  20, 2024, Judge Estudillo declined to voluntarily recuse and referred the motion to this Court for 

5  decision. See Dkt. No. 292 at 5.                                          
6                         II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                
7       Local Civil Rule (“LCR”) (3)(f) requires a challenged judge to review motions filed 
8  pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 144 or 28 U.S.C. § 455 and to determine whether to recuse voluntarily. 
9  LCR 3(f). If the challenged judge declines to recuse voluntarily, the judge must direct the court 
10  clerk to refer the motion to the chief judge for their review. Id. If the motion is directed at the 
11  chief judge, or if the chief judge (or their designee) is unavailable, the clerk must refer the 
12  motion to the active judge with the highest seniority. Id.                
13       28 U.S.C. § 455(a) provides that judges of the United States “shall disqualify [themselves 
14  in any proceeding in which [their] impartiality might reasonably be questioned.” The statute 

15  further provides that judges must recuse “[w]here [they have] a personal bias or prejudice 
16  concerning a party, or personal knowledge of disputed evidentiary facts concerning the 
17  proceeding.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(1). Similarly, 28 U.S.C. § 144 requires recusal when “a party to 
18  any proceeding in a district court makes and files a timely and sufficient affidavit that the judge 
19  before whom the matter is pending has a personal bias or prejudice either against [them] or in 
20  favor of any adverse party.” The standard for recusal under both statutes is the same: “Whether a 
21  reasonable person with knowledge of all the facts would conclude that the judge’s impartiality 
22  might reasonably be questioned.” United States v. McTiernan, 695 F.3d 882, 891 (9th Cir. 2012) 
23  (internal citation omitted). “The alleged prejudice must result from an extrajudicial source; a 

24  judge’s prior adverse ruling is not sufficient cause for recusal.” United States v. Studley, 783 
1  F.2d 934, 939 (9th Cir. 1986) (internal citation omitted); see also Liteky v. United States, 510 
2  U.S. 540, 555 (1994) (“[J]udicial rulings alone almost never constitute a valid basis for a bias or 
3  partiality recusal motion.”) (internal citation omitted).                 
4                            III.  DISCUSSION                                

5       As an initial matter, this motion is before this Court because Chief Judge David Estudillo 
6  referred the motion pursuant to Local Civil Rule 3(f). Dkt. No. 292 at 5. 
7       In seeking Judge Estudillo’s recusal, Mr. Bayley references some comments he heard 
8  Judge Estudillo make at a public presentation entitled “Not Lost in Translation: Innovations in 
9  Language Access” that was held on February 8, 2024. See generally Dkt. Nos. 289, 290. Mr. 
10  Bayley states that he heard Judge Estudillo discuss the importance of “effective communication, 
11  parties feeling heard and understood, unwavering respect owed to all parties and equal access to 
12  justice.” Dkt. No. 289 at 2. Yet, Mr. Bayley feels that “the Chief Judge either ignores 
13  Defendants’ arguments or brushes them off without effectively communicating in a manner that 
14  makes the Defendant feel heard, understood, or respected and that their arguments have been 

15  fully considered by the Court.” Id. at 3–4. In particular, Mr. Bayley asserts that Judge Estudillo 
16  did not adequately consider Defendants’ arguments and authorities. Id. at 3; see also Dkt. No 293 
17  at 1–2; Dkt. No. 295 at 2. While it is regrettable that Mr. Bayley does not feel adequately heard 
18  or understood, his challenge essentially boils down to a disagreement with Judge Estudillo’s 
19  rationale in his rulings and how he applied the law to the facts in this case. But “a judge’s prior 
20  adverse ruling is not sufficient cause for recusal.” Studley, 783 F.2d at 939. The basis for recusal 
21  generally requires something other than judicial rulings or “opinions formed by the judge on the 
22  basis of facts introduced or events occurring in the course of the current proceedings.” Liteky, 
23  510 U.S. at 554-56; accord United States v. Holland, 519 F.3d 909, 913–14 (9th Cir. 2008). 

24                                                                            
1  “Almost invariably,” rather than a basis for recusal, judicial rulings are a basis for appeal. Id. at 
2  555.                                                                      
3       To the extent Mr. Bayley asserts that comments Judge Estudillo made at the public 
4  presentation are an extrajudicial source that revealed a “lack of impartiality between the parties 

5  in this case” (Dkt. No. 289 at 1), it is unclear how any of the comments cited by Mr. Bayley in 
6  his declaration (Dkt. No. 290)2 would call into question Judge Estudillo’s impartiality in this 
7  case, especially since no interpreters appear to be involved in this case at all. Cf. McTiernan, 695 
8  F.3d at 891 (stating the standard for determining whether recusal is warranted). Mr. Bayley also 
9  asserts that Judge Estudillo “has weaponized his Western Washington District Court and all 
10  active status subordinate judges to enact his prejudices.” Dkt. No. 289 at 5; see also Dkt. No. 295 
11  at 1 (contending that “the entire United States District Court Western District of Washington is 
12  compromised, weaponized, and polluted with his prejudices and instructions to his subservient 
13  judges to deploy vindictive retaliations”). The only potential example he gives is that Judge 
14  Estudillo has “brag[ged] about weaponizing Judge Tana Kim (whom his [sic] own comments 

15  should disqualify her from weighing in on his denial of my motion to recuse him).” Dkt. No. 
16  293 at 3 (emphasis in original); Dkt. No. 295 at 4 (same). First, Mr. Bayley did not specify the 
17  comments “Tana Kim” made that should disqualify her from ruling on the present motion. 
18  Second, the undersigned believes Mr. Bayley has referenced her in his statement about “Tana 
19  Kim.” However, it appears that Mr. Bayley has confused the undersigned judge (Tana Lin) with 
20  an interpreter who was a panelist at the public presentation (Eunyoung Kim). See Dkt. No. 292 at 
21                                                                            
22                                                                            

   2 No audio or video of the presentation is available, so the Court will accept the accuracy of Mr. Bayley’s 
23                                                                            
   representations regarding comments made by Judge Estudillo for purposes of this motion to recuse. However, the 
   fact that only small excerpts are included make it difficult to determine if Mr. Bayley’s interpretation of the 
24  comments are either mistaken or perhaps taken out of context.             
1  3–4. The undersigned did not attend, participate in, or make any comments at the public 
2  presentation at issue.                                                    
3                           IV.  CONCLUSION                                  
4       Having considered Mr. Bayley’s arguments in support of recusal and finding them 

5  without merit, this Court AFFIRMS Judge Estudillo’s order denying Mr. Bayley’s motion to 
6  recuse.                                                                   
7       Dated this 27th day of February 2024.                                
8                                                                            
                                      A                                      
9                                                                            
                                      Tana Lin                               
                                      United States District Judge
